concepts.title: power spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The light intensity at each wavelength is called the power spectrum of the light.
concepts.content: The light intensity at each wavelength is called the **power spectrum** of the light. The color appearance of light is determined by many factors, including the image context in which the light is viewed; but a very important factor in determining color appearance is the power spectrum. In this initial discussion of color, we will assume that the power spectrum of light determines its appearance, although you should remember that this is true only within a fixed visual context.
concepts.motivation_md: The power spectrum quantifies light intensity across wavelengths, serving as a fundamental factor in determining perceived color under consistent viewing conditions.
concepts.recap_md:
- Power spectrum is the light intensity at each wavelength.
- Color appearance depends on power spectrum and viewing context.
- Initial color discussions often assume power spectrum determines appearance.

concepts.title: bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF)
concepts.one_liner: The reflection of light from a surface is described by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF).
concepts.content: The interaction between light and a surface can be quite complex. Reflections can be specular or diffuse, and the reflected power spectrum may depend on the relative orientations of the incident light, surface, and the observed reflected ray. In its full generality, the reflection of light from a surface is described by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) @Nicodemus1965, @Matusik2002. For this discussion, we will focus on diffuse surface reflections, where the power spectrum of the reflected light, $r(\lambda)$, is proportional to the wavelength-by-wavelength product of the power spectrum of the incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and a **reflectance spectrum**, $s(\lambda)$, of the surface:
concepts.motivation_md: BRDF models how light reflects off surfaces in different directions and spectra, enabling accurate rendering and analysis of surface appearance.
concepts.recap_md:
- BRDF describes how light reflects from surfaces.
- Reflection can be specular or diffuse.
- Reflected power spectrum depends on incident light and surface orientation.

concepts.title: reflectance spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The reflectance spectrum of a surface scales the incident light's power spectrum wavelength-by-wavelength to produce the reflected light's power spectrum.
concepts.content:
Incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and a **reflectance spectrum**, $s(\lambda)$, of the surface:
$$r(\lambda) = k \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) s(\lambda),$$ 

where the proportionality constant $k$ depends on the reflection geometry. This diffuse reflection model characterizes most matte reflections. Such wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is also a good model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through an attenuating filter. The incident power spectrum is then multiplied at each wavelength by the **transmittance spectrum** of the attenuating filter.
concepts.motivation_md: The reflectance spectrum models how surfaces modify incident light's spectrum to produce reflected light, crucial for understanding color and appearance.
concepts.recap_md:
- Reflected light spectrum $r(\lambda)$ equals incident spectrum times reflectance spectrum times $k$.
- $k$ depends on reflection geometry.
- Model applies to matte reflections and spectral changes by filters.

concepts.title: Spatial Resolution and Color
concepts.one_liner: Color interacts with our perception of spatial resolution, with the eye sensitive to fine spatial modulations in some color directions but relatively insensitive in others.
concepts.content:
Color interacts with our perception of spatial resolution. For some directions in color space, the eye is very sensitive to fine spatial modulations, while for other color space directions, the eye is relatively insensitive. Some color coordinate systems take advantage of this disparity to enable efficient representation of images by sampling image data sparsely along color axes where human perception is insensitive to blurring.

In a red-green-blue (RGB) representation, the eye is sensitive to high spatial frequency changes in both red and green, as shown in figures @fig-girls1 and @fig-girls2. A rotation of the color coordinates of the image, followed by a nonlinear stretching, can put the image into a color space called L, a, b. In that space, the eye is very sensitive to any blurring of the L color component, called luminance, but is relatively insensitive to blurring of the a or b components, as demonstrated in @fig-girls3 and @fig-girls4. This effect is commonly exploited in image compression, allowing some image components to be sampled more coarsely than others.

(see figure: (a) Original image. (b) RGB components. (c) RGB components, each blurred. These sharp and blurred components are used in the color images of @fig-girls2)

(see figure: Color images composed of sharp and blurred components from figures @fig-girls1 (b) and @fig-girls1 (c). (a) R component blurred, G and B components sharp. (b) G component blurred, R and B components...)

(see figure: (a) Original image. (b) Lab components. (c) Lab components, each blurred. These sharp and blurred components are used in the color images of @fig-girls4)

(see figure: Color images composed of sharp and blurred components from figures @fig-girls3 (b) and @fig-girls3 (c). Fig (a) L component blurred, a and b components sharp. (b) a component blurred, L and b...)

- RGB space is sensitive to high-frequency changes in red and green.
- L, a, b space separates luminance (L) from color components (a, b), allowing efficient image compression.

concepts.title: Concluding Remarks
concepts.one_liner: The three classes of color sensors in our eyes project light spectra into a 3-dimensional color space, and humans observe different colors with different spatial resolutions.
concepts.content:
The three classes of color sensors in our eyes project light spectra into a 3-dimensional color space. While human perception of color depends on more than just the spectrum of the light being observed, most systems for color matching achieve good results by assuming that the spectrum is all that matters. Linear algebra can find the best controls for a display or printing device in order to match the color measured by a set of sensors.

As would be expected from the spatial varying pattern of color sensors in our eyes--we have few blue or short-wavelength sensors--humans observe different colors with different spatial resolutions, a fact that is exploited in image compression methods.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding how human color sensors work and their spatial resolution differences helps improve color matching and image compression techniques.
concepts.recap_md:
- Human eyes have three classes of color sensors projecting light spectra into 3D color space.
- Color perception depends mostly on light spectrum, enabling color matching.
- Spatial variation in sensors causes different spatial resolutions for colors, used in image compression.

concepts.title: Color Matching
concepts.one_liner: One of the tasks of color science is to predict when a person will perceive that two colors match.
concepts.content:
Color science tells us how to analyze and reproduce color. We seek to build image displays so that the output colors match those of some desired target, and to manufacture items with the same colors over time. Much of the color industry revolves around the ability to repeatably control colors. Colors can be trademarked (Kodak Yellow, IBM Blue) and we have color standards for foods. @fig-french shows French fry color standards.

(see figure: The USDA color standards for French fried potatoes, one of many color standards @Munsell2020)

One of the tasks of color science is to predict when a person will perceive that two colors match. For example, we want to know how to adjust a display to match the color reflecting off some colored surface. Even though the spectra may be very different, the colors can almost always be made to match.

It is possible to infer human color matching performance by examining the spectral sensitivity curves of the receptors shown in @fig-ramon (b). We attempt to match a color using a combination of reference colors, typically called primary colors. Through experimentation, it has been discovered that the appearance of any color can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors. This is due to the presence of three classes of photoreceptors in our eyes. It has also been found that these color matches are transitive---if color A matches a particular combination of primaries and color B matches the same combination of primaries, then color A will match color B. Consequently, the amount of each primary required to match a color can serve as a set of coordinates indicating color @Wandell95.
concepts.motivation_md: Color matching enables consistent reproduction and control of colors in displays and manufacturing, ensuring that colors appear the same to human observers despite differences in spectra.
concepts.recap_md:
- Color science seeks to reproduce colors so outputs match desired targets.
- Any color can be matched by a linear combination of three primary colors due to three photoreceptor classes.
- Color matches are transitive, allowing coordinates based on primary amounts to represent colors.

concepts.title: Color Metamerism
concepts.one_liner: Two different spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes.
concepts.content: Two different spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes. There is a large space of metamers: any two vectors describing light power spectra that give the same projection onto a set of color matching functions will look the same to our eyes. There's a high-dimensional space of light spectra, and we're only viewing projections onto a 3D subspace in the colors we see.
concepts.motivation_md: Metamerism explains why different spectral compositions can look identical, highlighting the importance of color matching functions in color perception.
concepts.recap_md:
- Metameric spectra look the same color despite different spectral power distributions.
- Color perception projects high-dimensional spectra onto a 3D subspace.
- Metamers share identical projections onto color matching functions.

concepts.title: Linear Algebraic Interpretation of Color Matching
concepts.one_liner: The task of color measurement is to find the projection of a given light spectrum into the special 3D subspace defined by the eye's cone spectral response curves.
concepts.content:
In this chapter, we assume that color appearance is determined by the light spectrum reaching the eye. In reality, numerous factors can influence color appearance, including the eye's state of brightness adaptation, ambient illumination, and surrounding colors. However, a color matching system that relies solely on the light spectrum will still perform well.

To measure the color associated with a light spectrum \(\mathbf{t}\) we need to be able to predict the eye's responses to the spectrum. From equation (@eq-lmsct), the task of color measurement is to find the projection of a given light spectrum into the special 3D subspace defined by the eye's cone spectral response curves. Any basis for that 3D subspace will serve that task, so the three basis functions do not need to be the color sensitivity curves of @fig-ramon themselves. They can be any linear combination of them, as well.

We can define a **color reproduction system**, @fig-colorsystem, by first specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves. We put these into the \(3 \times N\) matrix, \(\mathbf{C}\), where \(N\) is the number of spectral samples over the visible illumination range. As discussed previously, the three curves, \(\mathbf{C}\), should be a linear combination of the eye's spectral sensitivity curves, or
$$
\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \, \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}},
$$
where \(\mathbf{R}\) is any full-rank \(3 \times 3\) matrix. We can translate between any two different color spaces by applying a general \(3 \times 3\) matrix transformation to change basis vectors. Note, the basis vectors do not need to be orthogonal, and most color system basis vectors are not.

(see figure: A color reproduction system. Light sensors a, b, and c respond to the input light spectrum \(\mathbf{t}\), giving sensor activations \(\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}\). Combinations of those activations drive the...)

### Color Matching Functions and Primary Lights

A color reproduction system measures an input light and produces an output light that matches the color appearance of the input light. A camera with a screen display is an example of a color reproduction system, as the colors of objects in the world are measured, then reproduced on the screen display of the camera. We can match the eye's response to a given light spectrum through the appropriate control of a sum of three lights, which we'll call the **primary lights**. For the example of a display screen, the three color elements of each pixel are the primary lights.

Because the eye's photosensors respond in linear proportion to the amount of the incoming light spectrum within its spectral sensitivity curve, the rules of linear algebra apply to color manipulation. For a given set of three primary lights, the strengths of each primary light can be adjusted to obtain a visual match to a desired color. There is one exception to this: because primary lights can only be combined in positive values, some input colors are outside the **gamut**---the range of colors that can be produced---of a the positive combination of a given set of primary lights.

The color reproduction system is then defined by two sets of spectral curves and a \(3 \times 3\) matrix, \(\mathbf{M}\), see @fig-colorsystem. The first set are the spectral sensitivities as a function of wavelength for each of the three photosensors. We write each of those spectral curves as a row vector of a matrix, \(\mathbf{C}\). The \(3 \times 3\) matrix, \(\mathbf{M}\), translates any color measurement to a set of amplitude controls for the primary lights, \(\mathbf{P}\). The second set of spectral curves of a color reproduction system are the spectra of the three primary lights, which we write as column vectors of the matrix, \(\mathbf{P}\).

For a given set of primary lights, \(\mathbf{P}\), we seek to find a matrix of color sensitivity curves, \(\mathbf{C}\), and \(3 \times 3\) matrix, \(\mathbf{M}\), which allow perfect reproduction of colors, as viewed by a human observer. Here, we derive the conditions that \(\mathbf{P}\), \(\mathbf{C}\), and \(\mathbf{M}\) must satisfy to allow for perfect reproduction of colors.

Let the spectrum of the light reflecting from the surface to be matched in color be \(\mathbf{t}\). The eye's response to that light is modeled as the sum of a term-by-term multiplication of the spectral sensitivities of each photoreceptor, in the rows of \(\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}\) times the spectrum of the light. Thus, the responses of the eye to that spectrum will be the \(3 \times 1\) column vector, \(\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}} \mathbf{t}\).

We can write the response of the eye to the *output* of the color matching system as the following matrix products. The light impinging on the sensors (a, b, c in @fig-colorsystem) of the color matching system will give responses \(\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}\) and controls \(\mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}\) to the primary lights. If this output modulates the corresponding primary lights (d, e, and f in @fig-colorsystem), then the light displayed by the color matching system will be \(\mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}\). We want this spectrum to give the same responses in the eye as the original reflected color, thus we must have:
\(\mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{t}\).
Because that relation must hold for *any* input vector \(\mathbf{t}\), we must have
$$
\mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C}  = \mathbf{C}_{eye}   
$$

What conditions on \(\mathbf{P}\) and \(\mathbf{C}\) are required for equation (@eq-match) to hold? First, the subspace of the eye responses \(\mathbf{C}_{eye}\) must be the same as that measured by the color sensing system, \(\mathbf{C}\). If that weren't the case, then perceptibly different spectra could map onto the same color sensing system measurements. So we must have
\(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{C}_{eye}\), for some full-rank \(3 \times 3\) matrix, \(\mathbf{R}\) (with inverse \(\mathbf{R}^{-1}\)). Substituting this twice into equation (@eq-match) gives
$$
\mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{C}_{eye} = \mathbf{C}_{eye}
$$ 
From @eq-match2 it follows that \(\mathbf{C} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I}_3\), the \(3 \times 3\) identity matrix. These conditions on the spectral sensitivities, \(\mathbf{C}\), the display spectra, \(\mathbf{P}\) and the sensors-to-primaries mixing matrix, \(\mathbf{M}\) for a color reproduction system are summarized below: 

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{C} &= \mathbf{R} \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}} 
\end{aligned}
$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{M} &= (\mathbf{C P})^{-1},
\end{aligned}
$$

where \(\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}\) are the human photoreceptor sensitivities and \(\mathbf{R}\) is a full-rank \(3 \times 3\) matrix.

concepts.title: color reproduction system
concepts.one_liner: We can define a color reproduction system by specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves in a $3 \times N$ matrix $\mathbf{C}$.
concepts.content:
We can define a **color reproduction system**, @fig-colorsystem, by first specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves. We put these into the \(3 \times N\) matrix, \(\mathbf{C}\), where \(N\) is the number of spectral samples over the visible illumination range. As discussed previously, the three curves, \(\mathbf{C}\), should be a linear combination of the eye's spectral sensitivity curves, or
$$
\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \, \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}},
$$
where \(\mathbf{R}\) is any full-rank \(3 \times 3\) matrix. We can translate between any two different color spaces by applying a general \(3 \times 3\) matrix transformation to change basis vectors. Note, the basis vectors do not need to be orthogonal, and most color system basis vectors are not.

concepts.title: Color Matching Functions and Primary Lights
concepts.one_liner: A color reproduction system measures an input light and produces an output light that matches the color appearance of the input light.
concepts.content:
A color reproduction system measures an input light and produces an output light that matches the color appearance of the input light. A camera with a screen display is an example of a color reproduction system, as the colors of objects in the world are measured, then reproduced on the screen display of the camera. We can match the eye's response to a given light spectrum through the appropriate control of a sum of three lights, which we'll call the **primary lights**. For the example of a display screen, the three color elements of each pixel are the primary lights.

Because the eye's photosensors respond in linear proportion to the amount of the incoming light spectrum within its spectral sensitivity curve, the rules of linear algebra apply to color manipulation. For a given set of three primary lights, the strengths of each primary light can be adjusted to obtain a visual match to a desired color. There is one exception to this: because primary lights can only be combined in positive values, some input colors are outside the **gamut**---the range of colors that can be produced---of a the positive combination of a given set of primary lights.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding color matching functions and primary lights is essential for reproducing colors accurately in devices like displays and cameras.
concepts.recap_md:
- Color reproduction systems match input light colors by producing output lights.
- Primary lights are three lights combined to match colors.
- Some colors lie outside the gamut of positive combinations of primary lights.

concepts.title: CIE Color Space
concepts.one_liner: The CIE color space is defined by three color sensitivity functions that are linear combinations of the eye's sensitivities.
concepts.content:
A color space is defined by the matrix, \(\mathbf{C}\), with three rows of color sensitivity functions. These three sensitivity functions, \(\mathbf{C}\), must be some linear combination of the sensitivity functions of the eye, \(\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}\). One color standard is the Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage (CIE) *XYZ* color space, \(C_{\mbox{CIE}}\). The CIE color matching functions, the rows of \(\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{CIE}}\) were designed to be all-positive at every wavelength and are shown in @fig-ciecie.

(see figure: CIE color matching functions @cie1931)
concepts.motivation_md: The CIE color space provides a standardized, all-positive basis for color representation, facilitating consistent color communication and reproduction.
concepts.recap_md:
- Color spaces are defined by three color sensitivity functions in matrix \(\mathbf{C}\).
- These functions are linear combinations of the eye's sensitivities.
- The CIE XYZ color space uses all-positive color matching functions.
